**A random hyperplane turns a direction into one bit.** Hash a nonzero vector according to which side of the hyperplane it lies on. Two vectors with a small angle are likely to land on the same side; opposite directions are unlikely to agree. [1](https://nlp.stanford.edu/IR-book/)

Restrict attention to the plane containing the two vectors. For isotropic random orientations, the fraction of separating hyperplanes is theta divided by pi. Thus bit agreement probability is $1-\theta/\pi$. At a 60-degree angle, one-bit agreement is two thirds.

**Several bits make stricter buckets.** With k independent bits, exact bucket collision probability is $(1-\theta/\pi)^k$. More bits reduce unrelated collisions but can also miss relevant neighbors. Multiple tables or probing nearby bit patterns increase recall at additional cost.

This collision formula is not the complete retrieval recall. Candidate budgets, table counts, reranking, and data geometry matter. Use angular conventions consistently and handle zero vectors explicitly. Compare the resulting latency–recall tradeoff with other ANN methods rather than assuming a mathematically elegant collision rule is automatically the fastest index.

**Technical details and references.**

Hash a vector by the sign of its dot product with a random isotropic hyperplane normal. Restrict attention to the two-dimensional plane spanned by two nonzero vectors with angle $\theta$. The hyperplane separates them for a fraction $\theta/\pi$ of equally likely orientations, so a single sign bit agrees with probability $1-\theta/\pi$. [1](https://nlp.stanford.edu/IR-book/)

Concatenating $k$ independent sign bits makes exact bucket collision probability $(1-\theta/\pi)^k$. Multiple tables increase recall at extra memory/query cost, while probing nearby bit strings trades extra work for fewer tables. Normalize or use angular distance consistently, handle zero vectors separately, and benchmark against HNSW or other ANN methods. The single-bit formula is not the full retrieval recall: candidate budgets, table count, and reranking all affect end-to-end performance.
